storyboard.claim: Auggie wears the heavy plastic astronaut helmet outside in blistering summer heat.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie standing outdoors, helmet on, happy and at ease — he is not suffering; he chose this.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Picks up the park image the hosts introduced — we now see Auggie actually wearing it.
storyboard.addedInformation: Happy expression signals comfort, not distress — the helmet is a pleasure, not a burden.

callout.text: wore it everywhere for two years

storyboard.claim: The helmet was a gift from Via's friend Miranda. Auggie wore it everywhere for two straight years.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie alone with the helmet on — ownership made clear; only he wore it.
storyboard.onScreenText: wore it everywhere for two years
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Adds origin story and duration to the helmet we just saw on his head.
storyboard.addedInformation: Via removed to avoid viewer inferring she also wore it.

storyboard.claim: Winter, summer, the beach — he loved it and felt safe inside it.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie on the shore with the helmet, completely at ease — the helmet is his world.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Extends scope across all seasons and names the emotional reason: safety.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shore set signals 'the beach' from the narration; happy face confirms 'he loved it.'

storyboard.claim: Contrast the safe helmeted kid with the moment Auggie walks into Tushman's office completely bare.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie walking into the principal's office, no helmet, face visible, visibly tense — the pivot from safety to exposure.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The pivot: from the safety image to the exposure moment.
storyboard.addedInformation: Tushman in the background grounds the school context.

storyboard.claim: The helmet is gone. Auggie meets Jack, Julian, and Charlotte for the first time — completely exposed.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie without the helmet, face bare, worried; Julian beside him seeing him for the first time.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Confirms the contrast: this is the scene without the shield.
storyboard.addedInformation: Julian placed second because the 'look away' dynamic begins with him immediately.

storyboard.claim: The kids instinctively dart their eyes to Auggie's face, then frantically look anywhere else — the 'look away thing.'
storyboard.concreteVisual: Julian with blank, avoidant expression beside Auggie — blank reads as deliberate non-engagement.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Immediate social consequence of Auggie entering without the helmet.
storyboard.addedInformation: Blank expression signals apathy / deliberate avoidance rather than cruelty.

storyboard.claim: The helmet was never just Auggie's shield — it was a psychological shield protecting everyone else from the discomfort of seeing his face.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Shield icon beside Auggie; callout flips the direction — it shielded others, not only him.
storyboard.onScreenText: shield for the rest of us
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The hosts reframe what the helmet meant: comfort flows both ways.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shield reads as protection; callout specifies the beneficiary is 'the rest of us.'

storyboard.claim: The helmet protected everyone from processing their discomfort. When it comes off, everyone's character is suddenly tested.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie without the helmet beside Jack — both exposed; the helmet icon marks what was removed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Consequence of the shield's removal falls on both sides.
storyboard.addedInformation: Neutral face shows this is a structural moment, not August's personal fear.

storyboard.claim: Without the helmet, everyone's character is suddenly violently on trial.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack and Julian side by side — visibly different (sandy hair vs. dark preppy), both surprised — their moral character now visible.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the stakes: it is not only Auggie being tested, it is every kid around him.
storyboard.addedInformation: Two distinct characters staged together so the viewer reads 'multiple people,' not one.

callout.text: just a kid in a costume

storyboard.claim: With the helmet on, people could smile — he was just a kid in a costume. Without it, they must confront his face and their own empathy.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie in the helmet, happy — the helmet makes him readable as a kid at play.
storyboard.onScreenText: just a kid in a costume
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why the helmet worked as a social shield: it gave others a comfortable story.
storyboard.addedInformation: Happy expression matches 'they could smile at him' — both parties were at ease.

storyboard.claim: The hosts pivot to the devastating detail: where did the helmet go?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie thinking, the astronautHelmet icon marking the absent object — the helmet is now a question.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Transition from the 'why it worked' analysis to the crucial plot reveal.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the question phrasing in the callout carries most of the tension.

storyboard.claim: For years, Auggie thought he simply lost the helmet.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie sad and thinking — quiet grief over something believed gone.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets up the gap between what Auggie believed and what actually happened.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sad + think reads as quiet grief, not shock — consistent with years of believing it was misplaced.

storyboard.claim: The truth: dad hid and threw away the helmet. Auggie is shattered when he finds out.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie slumped and devastated; helmet icon marks what was taken from him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The reveal lands: not lost — deliberately discarded.
storyboard.addedInformation: Slump reads as collapse/defeat — appropriate for 'shattered.'

storyboard.claim: Dad confesses: 'I couldn't stand seeing that thing cover your face anymore.'
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie and Isabel in quiet confrontation, the helmet icon marking the confessed object. Isabel talks; Auggie is sad.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The confession arrives — dad's words spoken; Isabel stands in for the parental voice.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: dad is not a defined cast member; Isabel carries the parental role by proximity.

callout.text: not good for him to hide

storyboard.claim: Dad's reasoning: it was not good for August to hide. This sparks the debate about parenting and protection.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Shield icon signals protection — the debate is whether hiding IS protection or harm. Isabel talking, Auggie worried.
storyboard.onScreenText: not good for him to hide
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Dad's justification — the other side of the betrayal claim.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shield + callout lets the viewer weigh 'protection' against 'hiding.'

storyboard.claim: One host says dad's action was incredibly cruel.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie slumped — the suffering child is the evidence for cruelty.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: First strong verdict in the debate — one host draws the line.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: staging shows the effect on the child, not the perpetrator.

callout.text: 27 surgeries before the cruelty even starts

storyboard.claim: This is a vulnerable child already poked, prodded, and cut open 27 times.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Medical icon + Auggie in hospital, afraid — 27 surgeries made literal.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Stakes the cruelty claim: look at what Auggie has already endured before any emotional betrayal.
storyboard.addedInformation: Medical reads as 'being treated / hospital' — accurate for 27 surgeries.

storyboard.claim: Auggie is stared at, pointed at, and whispered about every day. The helmet gave him a break from the relentless, aggressive public gaze.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie afraid on the street; Julian nearby as the embodiment of the staring public. Helmet icon marks the relief he lost.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Grounds the counter-argument: the helmet was a reasonable coping mechanism given daily exposure.
storyboard.addedInformation: Julian placed second as the representative 'public' who stares and looks away.

storyboard.claim: Stealing the helmet, throwing it away, then lying to his son for years is a massive betrayal.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mask icon signals the false face the dad wore for years; Auggie slumped in betrayal.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sharpens the argument: the theft was bad; the sustained lie is the betrayal.
storyboard.addedInformation: Mask reads as 'false public face' — the dad's years of deception fits exactly.

storyboard.claim: One host concedes: on a purely empathetic level, the other has a point about the suffering child.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Tushman (the adult authority figure) worried — an adult acknowledging an empathy argument, not a child experiencing something.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The host debate shifts — the pro-dad side concedes the empathy angle.
storyboard.addedInformation: Tushman replaces August so the viewer reads this as an adult debate concession, not as August's emotional experience.

storyboard.claim: The other host pushes back: how can you defend lying to a kid about his favorite toy?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie thinking, worried — the kid whose trust is the live question.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The concession is immediately challenged.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: host debate; Auggie is staged as the moral center of the argument.

storyboard.claim: Dad was the first person to realize August could not stay in a bubble. Taking the helmet was desperate, necessary tough love.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Isabel reaching toward Auggie — the parental act of intervention. Helmet icon marks the thing being taken, motivated by care.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The counter-argument crystallises: the lie was flawed, but the intention was survival.
storyboard.addedInformation: Reach with the helmet icon as subject prevents the action from reading as waving.

storyboard.claim: You cannot navigate the real world in a space suit. But the lie is a flaw — dad gaslighted his own kid.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie walking on the street without the helmet — navigating the real world; sad face acknowledges the cost.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The nuanced position: removal was right; the deception was wrong.
storyboard.addedInformation: Walk on street = 'navigating the real world' from the narration.

storyboard.claim: Parents are fallible, but the intention was survival.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Isabel thinking, worried — a parent wrestling with a hard choice.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Concedes the flaw but holds the intent.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: dad is not in the cast; Isabel carries the parental-decision weight.

storyboard.claim: Dad knew middle school was coming. The longer Auggie hid behind the plastic visor, the harder the eventual unveiling.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie with the helmet icon — the visor he is hiding behind. Afraid expression signals the cost of prolonged hiding.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Dad's foresight named: he saw the cliff ahead and removed the crutch before the fall.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the 'longer he hid' time element lives in the callout.

storyboard.claim: The helmet was like an atrophying muscle. Dad ripped off the bandage — painful, but necessary.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie slumped and afraid — the pain of removal. The callout carries the metaphor.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Metaphor for dad's method — the hosts agree it was painful.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the bandage metaphor is fully in the callout; staging shows the pain.

callout.text: IF YOU DONT EXPOSE A WOUND

storyboard.claim: Dad's heart had to shift first — stop mourning the 'normal' kid he expected and fiercely accept the reality.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Isabel slumped and sad — a parent's grief over the child they imagined.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The internal prerequisite before the external act: the parent's own acceptance.
storyboard.addedInformation: Isabel carries the parental grief; dad is not in the cast.

storyboard.claim: Without dad throwing away that helmet, Auggie never develops the thick skin required to survive Beecher Prep.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie walking confidently down the street, happy — the result. Helmet icon marks what was removed to make this possible.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The payoff of dad's gamble: Auggie navigating the world without the shield.
storyboard.addedInformation: Happy + walk contrasts with the slump of beats 52/55/65.

storyboard.claim: Robbing a vulnerable kid of their one safe space — the helmet — is reckless.
storyboard.concreteVisual: AstronautHelmet icon beside sad Auggie on abstract background — the protection that was taken.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Counter-counter-argument: even if removal was right, the method was reckless.
storyboard.addedInformation: AstronautHelmet icon instead of shield specifies the helmet as the safe space, preventing the room/home misread.

storyboard.claim: What if Auggie hadn't adapted? What if removing the helmet made him agoraphobic? Dad took a massive gamble with his son's mental health.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie slumped and afraid, helmet icon — the stakes of the gamble, the worst case that nearly was.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The risk named: the outcome was good, but it could have gone the other way.
storyboard.addedInformation: Afraid + slump stages the feared outcome.

storyboard.claim: The gamble paid off — dad understood the assignment and prepared August for the sorting mechanism of the real world.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie walking happy down the street — forward motion, world navigated.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Resolution of the risk: the debate tips toward dad's side.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: 'sorting mechanism' is abstract; the walking child is its result.

storyboard.claim: Now let's look closely at how adults actively manufacture the moral test for August.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Tushman talking — the adult architect of the arranged scenario.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: New thread: from dad's removal of the barrier to Tushman engineering the encounter.
storyboard.addedInformation: Tushman introduced as the engineer of what follows.

storyboard.claim: Tushman orchestrates a welcoming committee — calling in Jack, Julian, and Charlotte weeks before school starts.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Tushman pointing at Jack in the principal's office — the authority figure assigning the role.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The specific mechanism of adult manufacturing: names and action.
storyboard.addedInformation: Point reads as directing/assigning — Tushman giving Jack a duty.

storyboard.claim: Tushman's stated goal: easing August's transition into a mainstream school environment.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Road icon signals the path ahead; Auggie walking while Tushman watches — the transition being managed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Tushman's own words explain the strategy.
storyboard.addedInformation: Road reads as 'path forward' — fitting for a transition into a new environment.

storyboard.claim: Tushman genuinely thought the welcoming committee would teach the kids empathy, friendship, and loyalty.
storyboard.concreteVisual: chooseKindSign behind Tushman talking — the book's 'Choose Kind' ethos is what he is trying to install.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Tushman's good faith — his intent is real, even if the method is manufactured.
storyboard.addedInformation: Happy expression signals genuine belief, not manipulation.

storyboard.claim: The massive philosophical friction: arranged kindness by adults versus chosen kindness by kids.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Spectrum from 'Arranged kindness' to 'Chosen kindness' — the book's central tension in one line.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the structural conflict the next several beats will test.
storyboard.addedInformation: This is the book's thesis tension — a spectrum is the right diagram.

storyboard.claim: Adults are manufacturing a scenario — artificially forcing proximity between Auggie and the welcoming committee.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Tushman pointing toward Auggie — the adult imposing the encounter.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The left side of the spectrum named in action.
storyboard.addedInformation: Point reads as 'directing' — apt for an authority engineering contact.

storyboard.claim: You cannot manufacture genuine connection. Jack is honest about this in his own chapters.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack talking, happy — the genuine version of what Tushman could not engineer.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The right side of the spectrum — what must be chosen, not arranged.
storyboard.addedInformation: Jack introduced as the test case for genuine choice vs. assigned duty.

storyboard.claim: Jack admits he only hung out with August at first because Tushman asked him to — duty and intimidation from the principal.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack worried beside Tushman — the authority figure and the obligated kid.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Jack's starting point: arranged, not chosen.
storyboard.addedInformation: Worried expression on Jack signals discomfort/obligation rather than genuine warmth.

storyboard.claim: But then Jack's internal state actually shifts — it stops being a chore and he begins to genuinely choose it.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack thinking, now happy — the internal shift from obligation to genuine engagement.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The spectrum moves: arranged becomes chosen, happening inside Jack.
storyboard.addedInformation: Happy + think = someone deciding they actually want this.
